dossier.public_summary: The signal appears to be a 2.6 Earth-radius flat-bottom dip on average, but odd and even transits differ by ~90% and two deep transits are followed by two non-detections, including negative depths at 2-sigma. A second dip and extreme depth changes point to an eclipsing binary folded at twice the 14.6-day period rather than a planet.

reasons.why: Odd and even transits differ by almost a factor of 2 at 5 sigma, the classic signature of an eclipsing binary folded at half its true period (~29.2 d), not a planet at 14.6 d.
A second dip with positive SNR well above background appears near phase 0.4; depth 0.28 of the primary matches a stellar binary eclipse, not the tiny secondary a hot giant could show.

Depth is not constant: SPOC 2-min sector 20 2745 ppm and sector 47 -25 ppm (err 104), TESS-SPOC sector 60 -75 ppm (err 147) vs sectors 73 2254 ppm and 74 2613 ppm, also verified as changes_within_a_source with p_constant_all 2.8317749203922916e-81.

Individual transit depths are completely inconsistent (chi2 367.3 dof 5) with two deep events, two non-detections and share_of_top_3 1.0; 4 of 6 events are noise-level, inconsistent with a steady planet.

Flat-bottomed (v_sigma -3.16) and 2.6 Rearth alone would favour a planet, but in combination with odd/even differences, a real secondary, and a depth that flips from ~2600 ppm to undetected, a diluted EB at twice the period is the best explanation; size and shape alone do not disambiguate a blended flat eclipse.
